transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-20
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 45m
Attendees: Alex Monroe (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Jordan Hale (CTO - Lumen), Maya Chen (ML Eng - Lumen), Samir Patel (SRE - Lumen)

Summary:
Short walkthrough of Redwood Optimize quantization profiles, focusing on INT8 vs FP8 tradeoffs for Lumen's real-time summarization and batch embedding workloads. Agreed to run a 72-hour POC to compare quality vs latency and provide cost modeling. Action items and security docs to be shared.

Topics:
- Overview of quantization options (INT8, FP8) and Redwood default profiles
- Quality vs latency charts and examples
- Batch vs streaming behaviors and KV cache implications
- POC scope, dataset needs, and success criteria

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro, I'm Alex from Redwood, and Priya our SE will do the deep dive on Optimize quantization profiles.
[00:15] Jordan (CTO): Hey all, Jordan here. We're mainly looking to reduce inference costs for our summarization endpoint while keeping latency under 220ms p95 and minimal quality regression.
[00:28] Priya (SE): Great, thanks Jordan. So we'll walk through INT8 and FP8 profiles, typical quality delta numbers, and latency improvements. Note: some of the automatic transcribe might swap names, sorry for typos.
[00:42] Maya (ML Eng): Quick context: we run two production workloads — real-time summarization (short context, low latency) and nightly batch embeddings (longer context). We care about latency for the former, cost for the latter.
[01:05] Priya: Perfect. So INT8 generally gives the biggest cost reduction but can introduce ~1-3% quality loss on generative tasks depending on the model and prompt set. FP8 often hits a better quality/latency sweet spot — about 10-20% lower throughput improvement vs INT8 but with much smaller quality delta (~0.5-1%).
[01:30] Samir (SRE): Are there differences for streaming vs batch? We stream responses for summarization.
[01:38] Priya: Yes. Streaming still benefits from quantization but gains depend on kernel availability and sequence length. For short streaming sequences, batching effect is limited; however, Redwood's KV cache + prefix caching reduces repeated compute. Note, sometimes transcript shows K-V cash instead of KV cache.
[02:05] Alex: I'll jump in with a quick benchmark slide — Priya ran tests on a 13B-style open model. Baseline FP32 latency p95 for single-shot was ~260ms; INT8 brought that to ~180ms, FP8 to ~200ms. On quality evals (ROUGE/semantic sim), INT8 saw a small drop on certain prompts.
[02:35] Jordan: Those absolute numbers look promising. For our requirement 220ms p95, FP8 seems safe but INT8 would be even better if quality holds. How do you measure "quality" here?
[02:50] Priya: We use a blend: automated metrics (ROUGE, BLEU when relevant, embedding similarity) plus a small human eval for edge cases. For the POC we'll run the customer's prompt set through our eval harness and flag regressions above a threshold.
[03:12] Maya: About hallucination — did you see any increase with INT8?
[03:18] Priya: In our samples, hallucination increased slightly on abstractive prompts — maybe from model truncation and token distribution shifts. That's why we recommend running the actual prompt suite. Sometimes reranking helps mitigate hallucination at small cost.
[03:40] Samir: Ops concern — how stable are these profiles over model versions? I.e., we don't want a rollout to break.
[03:49] Alex: Good point. Redwood supports version pinning and rollouts — canary, A/B, automatic fallback to a compatible profile. We'll capture perf and quality baselines and create a rollback policy.
[04:05] Jordan: Security and compliance — we need SOC2 + KMS integration for customer keys.
[04:12] Alex: We will share the SOC2/ISO certs and KMS integration doc. For Private deployments we can support HSM/KMS and audit logs as needed.
[04:27] Priya: Back to quantization — practical tip: for summarization with short contexts, INT8 often gives the most latency wins because the compute dominates; for long-context embedding runs, FP8 can be better because it preserves more numeric dynamic range and reduces edge-case regressions.
[04:50] Maya: Could you show an example prompt and the difference in outputs between FP32/FP8/INT8?
[04:56] Priya: Sure, we have a screen share. Example prompt: "Summarize the following meeting notes focusing on action items and owners".
[05:10] [screen share noises, transcription imperfect]
[05:20] Priya: FP32 output — preserves fine-grained distinctions, mentions all action items. FP8 — almost identical, maybe one paraphrase. INT8 — condensed, missed a low-salience item in one sample. Again, depends on prompt wording.
[05:50] Jordan: Hmm. If we miss low-salience items that could be bad for compliance. Could reranking or post-filtering help?
[05:58] Priya: Yes, reranking or applying a simple heuristic check can recover those. Also prefix/KV caching means repeated similar prompts fare better.
[06:15] Samir: For the POC, we need to run 72-hour continuous load — is that doable on Redwood Dedicated?
[06:23] Alex: Absolutely. We can provision Dedicated capacity for the POC or run it on hosted with reserved throughput. We'll provide a pricing sheet for both.
[06:35] Priya: Walkthrough of the recommended profile: start with FP8 for canary on summarization to validate quality. If metrics good, we can try INT8 with canary + human eval gating. For embeddings, try INT8 for batch jobs where latency isn't strict; if quality regresses, move to FP8.
[06:58] Jordan: What's the expected cost delta? Rough estimates?
[07:03] Alex: Ballpark: FP8 ~30-40% cost reduction vs FP32; INT8 ~50-70% depending on utilization and batching. Nightly batch jobs usually see the higher end of those savings. We'll include modeled numbers in the template.
[07:25] Maya: How much instrumentation will we need to add? We already send traces to Datadog.
[07:32] Priya: Minimal — Redwood Console exposes per-route token cost, latency histograms, and per-model quality regressions. You can integrate traces and set alerts. We'll share dashboard samples.
[07:48] Jordan: Any gotchas for on-prem/private deploys?
[07:52] Priya: The main items are kernel availability for specific GPU types and quantization libraries. If you're on certain older GPUs, FP8 kernels might be limited; INT8 has broader support. We'll check your hardware matrix in the POC intake.
[08:10] Samir: We use A100 and some T4s for edge.
[08:15] Priya: A100 is fine for FP8; T4s will do INT8 but FP8 support is patchy. We'll recommend a mixed profile or routing policy to send critical low-latency requests to A100-backed Dedicated nodes.
[08:35] Alex: Quick recap: POC to run benchmarks, we share security docs and pricing, Priya will provide configs, Maya will provide dataset snippets.
[08:46] Jordan: Timeline — we'd like to start the POC next week.
[08:50] Alex: Can we target 2026-08-27 for kickoff?
[08:53] Jordan: Yes.
[08:55] Priya: I'll prepare the recommended INT8/FP8 configs and the eval harness instructions.
[09:03] Maya: I'll send sample prompts and a small dataset slice by Monday.
[09:10] Samir: I'll coordinate infra for Dedicated versus hosted benchmark.
[09:15] Alex: Great. Any other questions?
[09:20] Jordan: One more — competitors. Do you see similar quality with Cohere/Anthropic?
[09:27] Priya: We benchmark across open models and sometimes vendor models; results vary. We'll share relative charts but the key is testing with your prompts.
[09:40] Alex: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the action items.

End of transcript.
